items.prompt: StreamCast's chat backend averages 500 msgs/sec, and its live-event peak measured after the fact was 3,800 msgs/sec. Which number should a throughput budget be sized against?
choices: The average (500)
The peak (3,800)
Whichever number is easiest to remember
The provisioned capacity someone guessed
items.explanation: A throughput budget names the traffic a system must survive, and that's the peak, not the average — average traffic tells you what a typical day costs to run, not what a busy day requires.
items.reference:
📊 Average — typical day, not the target
🎫 Peak — what the system must survive
🖥️ Provisioned — what was guessed, not measured

Why: a throughput budget is derived from measured or forecast peak traffic — sizing off the average, or off an untested guess at per-server capacity, both understate what a system actually has to survive.

items.prompt: A service's fleet was provisioned to '600 msgs/sec' based on someone's guess of '100 msgs/sec per server times 6 servers.' Is that guessed number a valid throughput budget?
choices: Yes, guesses from experienced engineers are usually reliable
No — it wasn't derived from a measured or forecast peak, or actually tested
Yes, as long as the arithmetic is correct
No, because 6 servers is inherently too few
items.explanation: A number's validity as a throughput budget comes from where it's derived from — a measured or forecast peak, ideally backed by a real load test — not from whether the multiplication was done correctly on top of a guess.
items.reference:
📊 Average — typical day, not the target
🎫 Peak — what the system must survive
🖥️ Provisioned — what was guessed, not measured

Why: a throughput budget is derived from measured or forecast peak traffic — sizing off the average, or off an untested guess at per-server capacity, both understate what a system actually has to survive.

The traffic rate a system must be provisioned to survive, derived from peak — not average — traffic
The number of servers a team happens to already own
The total requests served across a full day
items.explanation: A throughput budget is specifically about the peak a system has to survive, not a description of typical daily traffic or existing infrastructure.
items.reference:
📊 Average — typical day, not the target
🎫 Peak — what the system must survive
🖥️ Provisioned — what was guessed, not measured

items.prompt: A request has a 50ms p99 time limit and passes through 5 hops. What does an explicit 'latency budget' mean in this context?
choices: Each hop can take as long as it wants as long as the average stays under 50ms
The 50ms is explicitly divided across the hops so each owner knows their real margin
Only the slowest hop needs to be measured
Latency budgets only apply to database queries
items.explanation: A latency budget is the discipline of dividing a total time limit across every hop a request passes through, so no hop's owner is left guessing how much time they actually have.
items.reference:
⏱️ Total SLA — e.g. 50ms p99, end to end
🔀 Each hop — gets an explicit share, not 'plenty'

Why: without an explicit split, every hop's owner assumes unlimited margin, and those assumptions don't have to add up to the real total.

items.prompt: Why does an explicit latency budget matter, instead of just having a single overall SLA number?
choices: Without dividing it across hops, every hop's owner tends to assume unlimited margin, and those assumptions don't have to add up to the real total
Because SLAs are only ever measured at the load balancer
Because a latency budget replaces the need for load testing
Because hops always run sequentially, so the total is always obvious
items.explanation: An overall SLA number alone doesn't tell any individual hop's owner what their real margin is — an explicit budget forces that split to be made on purpose, not assumed.
items.reference:
⏱️ Total SLA — e.g. 50ms p99, end to end
🔀 Each hop — gets an explicit share, not 'plenty'

Why: without an explicit split, every hop's owner assumes unlimited margin, and those assumptions don't have to add up to the real total.

items.prompt: Why doesn't a server running near 100% of its raw capacity fail gracefully?

Latency grows faster than load as headroom shrinks, and retries from slow requests pile on even more load
Servers at 100% utilization automatically shed excess load safely

items.explanation: As headroom disappears, each additional bit of load costs disproportionately more in latency, and clients retrying slow requests add real load on top of an already-struggling system — a small feedback loop that turns 'slow' into 'down.'
items.reference:
🧯 Headroom — the gap between actual load and raw capacity
📈 Near 0% headroom — latency grows faster than load, then retries pile on more

Why: running at ~100% of raw capacity doesn't fail gracefully — it fails suddenly, because latency and retries compound as headroom disappears.

items.explanation: Headroom is specifically the margin left between how much traffic a system is actually handling and the raw ceiling it could theoretically handle — distinct from the peak-to-average ratio, which describes the traffic pattern itself.
items.reference:
🧯 Headroom — the gap between actual load and raw capacity
📈 Near 0% headroom — latency grows faster than load, then retries pile on more

items.prompt: A request plan has hops A (5ms) and B (7ms) that run in parallel, followed by hop C (3ms) that waits for both to finish. What's the total latency?
choices: 15ms
10ms
12ms
7ms
items.explanation: Parallel branches cost the slowest one, not the sum: max(5, 7) + 3 = 10ms.

🔀 Parallel — cost is the slowest branch

items.prompt: Why does treating a parallel fan-out as if it were sequential (adding every branch's cost) produce a misleading latency estimate?

It overstates the real latency, since parallel branches finish together, not one after another
It understates the real latency, hiding real risk
Parallel fan-outs never affect a latency budget
items.explanation: Adding every parallel branch's cost double-(or triple-)counts time that actually elapses concurrently — the branches finish together, so only the slowest one determines when the fan-out is done.
items.reference:
➡️ Sequential — costs add up
🔀 Parallel — cost is the slowest branch

Why: confusing the two produces a wrong estimate in a predictable direction — sequential-izing a fan-out overstates the real total.

🔥 Under load — the same hops can cost far more

⏱️ Latency budget — does one request finish in time

items.prompt: Implement inflateForUtilization(nominalMs, utilization): clamp utilization to [0, 0.99], then return nominalMs * (1 + utilization / (1 - utilization)) — the illustrative queueing-inflation model used in this unit.

tests.description: 92% utilization multiplies the nominal cost by 12.5

items.explanation: The multiplier grows as utilization approaches 1 because it divides by the shrinking leftover room (1 − utilization) — at 92% utilization, only 8% room is left, so the multiplier is 1 + 0.92/0.08 = 12.5.
items.reference:
🔥 multiplier = 1 + ρ/(1−ρ)

Why: dividing by the shrinking leftover room is exactly what makes the same nominal cost balloon as utilization climbs toward 100%.

items.prompt: A fleet is under-provisioned and running near 100% utilization during a traffic spike. It drops to zero immediately
It doubles automatically whenever servers are added
It becomes irrelevant once any servers are added
items.explanation: The multiplier is a function of utilization, not raw server count — adding servers only helps if it actually lowers the utilization the fleet runs at. Adding capacity while keeping utilization just as high barely moves the multiplier.

🖥️ More servers — doesn't help by itself
🧯 Lower utilization — is what actually reduces the multiplier

Why: the inflation model depends on how close to 100% utilization the fleet runs, not on the raw server count.

items.prompt: Two teams both fix a latency SLA breach caused by high utilization. Team A adds servers but keeps running the fleet at 90% utilization. Team B adds the same number of servers and lowers target utilization to 65%. Whose fix reduces the queueing-inflation multiplier more?

Team A, because Team B's fleet has fewer total servers

items.reference:
🖥️ More servers — doesn't help by itself
🧯 Lower utilization — is what actually reduces the multiplier

Why: the inflation model depends on how close to 100% utilization the fleet runs, not on the raw server count.

Back-of-envelope math doesn't allow using historical data at all
items.explanation: A peak-to-average ratio is a property of a specific traffic pattern at a specific point in a product's life — treating it as a permanent constant ignores that growth, new features, and audience changes can shift it substantially.
items.reference:
📅 Measured once — from a single past event
🔁 Revisit it — as the platform and audience change

Why: a ratio measured under old conditions doesn't automatically hold as the system it describes keeps changing.
